items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: The interviewee discusses Joe Oliver extensively as a historical figure, quoting Johnny Dodds and Mutt Carey about Oliver's tone and band, but never claims a personal interaction or direct relationship with Oliver himself.

ctx.x: Well, you could tell me how American music got started. It started at the beginning.

So anyway, to get back to the point, Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities. You couldn't really tell much how he played, both because his lip wasn't in shape and just by himself. The type of trumpet playing that Bunk did, which was a remarkable thing, and yet by itself it wouldn't sound that effective. Bunk was hardly ever on the beat, so if you didn't hear him patting his foot and all there, you could really tell of course where the beat is, but…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: Then I heard about Louis Armstrong and King Oliver, and started trying to find their records.

ctx.x: I'm going to ask a real killer of a question. How did you ever get interested in jazz?

Well, I heard music when I was a kid, of course, like on the river boats and other places around town. I was raised in a small town on the Mississippi River. There wasn't any real jazz bands, but there used to be a few piano players, and especially on the boats I'd hear jazz. But I didn't really try to listen to it. I used to have the idea that it was... In fact, my violin teacher told me, don't try to play any of that music. It'll, you know, corrupt your style. I'll revile it. So, I did listen to records,…
Where'd you get, where would you get?

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: Yeah people like Johnny Wiggs and others have said that when the Oliver band stuff Records came down here, they didn't believe it was Oliver hardly, but it didn't sound like him. And I've heard that from other people too.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: The interviewee (William Russell) is narrating Jelly Roll Morton's opinions and stories about Joe Oliver (e.g., 'Jelly told him he'd heard more blues... The only other person that ever rivaled them was Joe Oliver... he had a lot of respect for Oliver'). There is no evidence in the transcript that Wi

ctx.x: What kind of music do you think they were playing? Would it differ in any way from say what they were playing in the middle 20s?

I would doubt it myself just from the evidence of people's styles not changing that rapidly. I can't, we don't have any records of them. Actually the original Dixieland was the first to record. It might have been of course they always called it ragtime. A lot has been made like for instance in Brun's book on Nick LaRocca always made a big point of that. That they were the first ones to use the word jazz. But not, I'm not trying to say the colored people were first or anything of that kind in this particular case…

You were talking about... Yeah, a lot of the Negroes down here, they're all crazy about him. They all try to imitate him. And yet occasionally you run across some of the old timers that'll say, well, he plays novelty music. It's not really good jazz.
